_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 3 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 4 Input Machines. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The six teaching chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (the input; the machine; the output; working it out; finding the rule; straight through, no choices), in the lesson's own words and with the lesson's own numbers. EVERY OUTPUT DRAWN IN THIS FILM COMES FROM ART.rule, the lesson's own ruleOutput mirrored in _rules.py, so the film's machines and the lesson's machines cannot disagree: double 3, double 5, add:3 of 10, add:8 of 4 and of 5, times:3 of 4 and of 5, add:4 of 3. The recipe's ingredients and the finished cake are the kit's own cake scene, painted from a growing list of its ids.
title: Input Machines
subtitle: Grade 3 Computing
objectives: Know how to develop linear algorithms to produce an output based on an input.
Know that logical thinking is used in the creation of algorithms.

beats.say: Put a number into a machine. Out comes a different number.
What goes in is the input. What comes out is the output.
Most algorithms start with an input: the thing they are given to work on.
A recipe's input is the ingredients. Eggs, flour and sugar go in.
A sum's input is the two numbers. Give it 3 and 4.
A search's input is the word you type. You type lions.
Robo's input is the program of arrows you give it.
The input is not a step. It is what the steps work on.
An algorithm can be a machine. Input in one side, output out the other.
In the middle are the steps. This is the doubling machine.
Take the number in. Add the number to itself. Send the answer out.
Put 3 in. 3 added to itself. Out comes 6, every time.
Put 5 in, and the same steps send 10 out instead.
The output is the result: the answer, the cake, the search results.
Make a cup of squash. Squash and water go in: they are the input.
Pour and stir are steps. The output is the cup at the end.
Same machine, a different input, a different output.
Once you know the steps, you can work out an output nobody has shown you.
Here is the add-3 machine. Take the number in, add 3 to it, send the answer out.
Put 10 in. What comes out? Follow the steps in your head.
13. You did not have to see it. That is logical thinking.
Sometimes nobody tells you the rule. You work it out yourself.
Put 4 in, and 12 comes out. What is the rule?
Add 8 fits that. Times 3 fits it too. So try another.
Put 5 in, and 15 comes out. Now add 8 is beaten.
Times 3 survives. One pair of numbers is never enough.
These machines are linear: no choices, just one step after another.
Input in. Step, step, step. Output out. Straight through.
Nothing in the middle asks a question. Nothing sends you a different way.
Later you will meet algorithms that ask questions. They take two routes.
The input goes in. The steps work on it. The output comes out.
The rule is what the machine does to whatever you give it.
Know the steps, and you can predict the output before you try it.
Same steps, a new input, a new answer.
